sections.overview: This Brazilian pit viper belongs to the diverse lancehead genus Bothrops, alongside the closely related B. fonsecai, another distinct pit viper of southern Brazil.
sections.identification: It has a stout body, a brown-to-grey ground colour with dark, broken trapezoid markings, a conspicuous dark V across the head and a nearly black belly; adults are commonly 70–80 cm, with exceptional specimens near one metre.
sections.habitat: It lives in cool highland forests of southern Brazil, including Araucaria woodland, a habitat that distinguishes it from many lowland lanceheads.
sections.diet: It preys on small mammals, especially rodents and marsupials, as recorded for this forest-dwelling lancehead in Brazilian species accounts.
sections.behavior: This terrestrial snake is mainly nocturnal and camouflaged in leaf litter, where its forest-floor habits can make it difficult to spot.
sections.reproduction: It bears live young, with summer litters of about 8–12 reported. A separate study found mating plugs and sperm storage in males.
sections.ecology: It belongs to the diverse lancehead genus Bothrops: the related B. fonsecai is another southern Brazilian highland viper, while B. jararaca is a useful comparison for head-scale pattern but is more broadly distributed.
sections.conservation: A regional Argentine database labels it rare in Misiones and cites an endangered assessment from 2012; older Brazilian state assessments also identify concern, but a current global category was not verified in the sources consulted.
